newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-New coal exporters to cut costs sharply-study.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-New coal exporters to cut costs sharply-study.

text.p: Sharp growth in low cost coal exports from Indonesia, Colombia and Venezuela will dramatically lower average world steaming coal costs in coming years, according to export coal study released on Monday.

The report by private commodities forecaster AME Mineral Economics said the three countries were expected to increase their share of global coal exports from 12.3 percent in 1995 to almost 20 percent by the year 2000.
Indonesia and Colombia were the lowest cost coal exporters in 1995, with South Africa joining low cost producers in 1996.
However, AME said export growth from emerging producers would not fully satisfy demand for steaming coal, which was being driven by Asian power needs.

Australia and the United States were the only two countries with the necessary export coal industry size, cost structure, and infrastructre to supply the remainder of the increased demand, the report said.
"Australia will continue to be the dominant coal exporting force over the next 10 years," it said.
Steaming coal demand was forecast to rise from about 285 million tonnes in 1996 to about 400 million tonnes in 2001.
Coking coal demand was seen rising from about 185 million tonnes to about 198 million tonnes over the same period.
AME said demand for coking coal continued to show resilience in the face of alternative steel making technologies.
However, supply would exceed demand, leading to the redirection of semi-coking coal into steaming markets.
Coal mining costs were expected to continue to fall in real terms due to improvements in mining technology, mine planning and mine management, the report said.
"The bad news for producers is that export coal prices will fall in line with costs, maintaining profit margins at near present levels," AME said.
Any lowering of margins would lead to a temporary cut in output, while any widening of margins would see additional capacity brought on-stream.
The study also noted that the international coal trade was moving toward a freer market.
"The Japanese benchmark system is dead for coking coal and on its last legs for steaming coal," it said.
Centralised and "transparent" trading markets, based on buy and sell transactions, could eventually be introduced for steaming coal, AME said.
